metadata.title: Relations between academic boredom, academic achievement, ICT use, and teacher enthusiasm among adolescents

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 public-use microdata from eight countries, where students are sampled via a two-stage design (stratified schools, then random student selection within schools). The authors state that the extracted samples are weighted to be representative of 15-year-olds enrolled in grade 7 or above, but they do not report the specific weight variable name(s) used in the analysis. The modeling strategy is multilevel (students nested in schools) and uses multiple imputation with plausible values, combining estimates using Rubin’s rules; this is consistent with respecting the complex sampling structure at the school level via multilevel modeling. The manuscript does not describe whether sampling weights were explicitly applied in the regression estimation; therefore, readers should treat the results as primarily multilevel-model-based rather than explicitly survey-weighted, unless the underlying PISA software defaults are known.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses use PISA 2018 public-use files restricted to the eight countries that administered both the well-being questionnaire (boredom) and the ICT familiarity questionnaire. The analytic sample includes students aged 15 years and 3 months to 16 years and 2 months (15-year-olds) enrolled in grade 7 or above, with cases extracted from the public-use files. The study further restricts achievement outcomes to reading and mathematics and matches boredom indicators to language-and-literature and mathematics contexts; reading achievement is not available for Spain due to implausible response behavior, so reading-based analyses exclude Spain for that domain. Missing data in modeling variables are handled via multiple imputation (ten imputation sets) combined with plausible values for achievement.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Reading and Mathematics — boredom in mathematics classes
top_predictors: ICT use for learning at home (activities)
ICT use for learning at home (subjects)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as ML metrics (multilevel linear probability-style models; standardized coefficients reported in text/figures). Effect sizes reported as standardized differences: ICT leisure +1 SD associated with ~11% of a SD in boredom in math classes on average; teacher enthusiasm +1 SD associated with −12% of a SD in boredom in math classes on average.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data from eight countries, the study leveraged ICT use for leisure, ICT use for learning at home (activities and subjects), perceived teacher enthusiasm, and socioeconomic status (ESCS) to model self-reported boredom in mathematics classes, finding that heavier ICT use for leisure is associated with higher boredom while teacher enthusiasm is associated with lower boredom. This indicates that strengthening classroom motivational climate (teacher enthusiasm) and managing leisure-oriented ICT use may help reduce boredom during mathematics instruction, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Reading and Mathematics — boredom in language and literature classes
main_findings.target_variable: Boredom in language and literature classes (self-reported)
top_predictors: ICT use for learning at home (activities)
ICT use for learning at home (subjects)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as ML metrics (multilevel linear models; standardized coefficients and marginal effects). Average effects reported: ICT leisure +1 SD associated with ~7% of a SD in boredom in language/literature; teacher enthusiasm +1 SD associated with −31% of a SD in boredom in language/literature. Moderation: ICT leisure increases boredom mainly among students who perceive teachers as not enthusiastic; ICT learning at home shows lower boredom among unenthusiastic-teacher students but weaker/flat associations among enthusiastic-teacher students.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data from eight countries, the study leveraged ICT use for leisure, ICT use for learning at home (activities and subjects), perceived teacher enthusiasm, and disciplinary climate (language) to model self-reported boredom in language and literature classes, finding that teacher enthusiasm strongly reduces boredom and moderates how ICT use relates to boredom. This indicates that teacher enthusiasm and classroom climate are key levers for buffering potential boredom risks associated with leisure-oriented ICT use, though causality cannot be inferred from the correlational, cross-sectional evidence.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Reading and Mathematics — boredom during self-study at home
top_predictors: ICT use for learning at home (activities)
ICT use for learning at home (subjects)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as ML metrics (multilevel linear models; standardized coefficients). Average effects reported: ICT leisure +1 SD associated with ~12% of a SD in boredom during self-study; teacher enthusiasm +1 SD associated with −11% of a SD in boredom during self-study. Moderation: among students who perceive teachers as enthusiastic, ICT learning at home does not meaningfully predict boredom; among unenthusiastic-teacher students, higher ICT learning at home is associated with lower boredom.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data from eight countries, the study leveraged ICT use for leisure, ICT use for learning at home (activities and subjects), perceived teacher enthusiasm, and reading achievement to model self-reported boredom during self-study at home, finding that leisure-oriented ICT use is associated with higher home-study boredom while teacher enthusiasm is associated with lower boredom. This indicates that improving teacher enthusiasm and aligning home ICT use with learning support may reduce boredom during independent study, while the study’s contemporaneous, cross-sectional nature limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 microdata from eight countries (Bulgaria, Georgia, Hong Kong, Ireland, Mexico, Panama, Serbia, Spain) to examine how academic boredom relates to achievement and how ICT use and teacher enthusiasm are associated with boredom among 15-year-olds. The authors model boredom in mathematics classes, language and literature classes, and self-study at home using multilevel models with students nested in schools, and they handle missing achievement data via multiple imputation combined with PISA plausible values using Rubin’s rules. They report standardized associations rather than ML performance metrics: ICT use for leisure shows positive associations with boredom (about +11% to +12% of a SD in math and self-study boredom on average), while teacher enthusiasm shows negative associations (about −12% in math, −31% in language/literature, and −11% in self-study on average). The key limitation is that the design is cross-sectional and correlational, so reverse causality and omitted-variable bias remain possible; additionally, the paper does not present survey-weight application details beyond stating weighted representativeness.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper is not an ML-prediction study, it uses multilevel regression with multiple imputation and plausible values; therefore, no machine-learning algorithms are evaluated and ml_techniques is intentionally left empty. The extraction focuses on the empirical associations reported in the Results section rather than predictive-model performance.
